title: Reverse an Array
directAnswer: Two pointers — `left = 0`, `right = n-1`. Swap `nums[left]` and `nums[right]`, then move both toward the centre until they cross. O(1) extra space.

remember.takeaway: Reverse-in-place = swap the ends and converge.
remember.formula: l=0; r=n-1; while l<r: swap(l,r); l++; r--

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, reverse it in place so the first element becomes the last.
understanding: Swap the two ends and walk both pointers inward until they meet.

approaches.name: Two-pointer swap
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Reverse in place with the **two-pointer swap**: `left` at the start, `right` at the end, swap them, and step both inward until they meet. O(n) time, O(1) extra space — no second array.

**Why pointers converge in the middle.** Each swap places two elements in their final positions, so after n/2 swaps every element is reversed. The middle element of an odd-length array is already in place and needs no swap — which is exactly why the loop condition is `left < right` (strictly), not `<=`.

**Why `<=` would be a bug.** With `left <= right`, the middle element would be swapped with itself (harmless), but more importantly on even lengths the pointers would cross and you'd swap the same pairs back, un-reversing the array. `left < right` stops cleanly when they meet or cross.

This swap-and-converge primitive underlies reverse-string and the three-reversal array rotation trick.
hints: Pair the first element with the last, second with second-last…
Two pointers from both ends; swap and move inward.
Stop when left meets right — use `<`, not `<=`.
approaches.insight: The two-pointer swap is the reusable primitive behind reverse-string and the three-reversal rotation.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n/2 swaps, each O(1), with only a temp variable — linear time, constant space.

java.explanation: Stop when the pointers meet — the middle element needs no swap.
Classic three-line swap of the two ends.

pitfalls: Looping the full length and swapping every pair twice (undoing the reversal).
Off-by-one: right starting at length instead of length − 1.

commonMistakes: Looping the full length and swapping twice (undoing the reversal).
Off-by-one in the right pointer (`n` instead of `n-1`).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reverse in place with two pointers and get the loop bound right.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Swapping across the whole array (double swap) or an out-of-bounds right pointer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In place or return a new array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place with two pointers for O(1) space; I can return a copy if required.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Swapping the full length
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping i from 0 to n−1 and swapping nums[i] with nums[n−1−i] swaps every pair twice, leaving the array unchanged.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) swap(nums, i, n-1-i);   // double swap
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int l = 0, r = n-1; while (l < r) { swap(nums, l++, r--); }
